steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptually, a transformer is a neural network architecture built around one key idea: instead of processing a sequence step by step, it lets every token in the sequence “look at” (attend to) every other token directly, all at once. Here are the essential pieces and how they fit together:

1. Embeddings  
   • Each input token (word, sub-word, character, etc.) is converted into a continuous vector.  
   • Positional information (so the model knows order) is added or encoded alongside these vectors.

2. Self-attention (the core mechanism)  
   • For every token, the model forms three learned vectors: a Query (Q), a Key (K), and a Value (V).  
   • It measures how well the Query of one token matches the Keys of every other token (a dot product), producing a set of attention weights.  
   • A softmax turns these scores into probabilities that sum to 1.  
   • Each token’s new representation is a weighted sum of the Value vectors, using those probabilities—so it gathers information from the whole sentence, focusing most on the parts deemed relevant.

3. Multi-head attention  
   • The Q/K/V computation is done several times in parallel with different learned projections (heads).  
   • Each head can capture different kinds of relationships (e.g., syntax, long-range context).  
   • The heads’ outputs are concatenated and linearly combined.

4. Feed-forward network  
   • After attention, each position passes through the same small two-layer MLP (with nonlinearity).  
   • This gives the model extra capacity to transform the attended information.

5. Add & Norm (residuals and normalization)  
   • A residual connection adds the input of each sub-layer (attention or feed-forward) to its output, helping gradients flow.  
   • Layer normalization then stabilizes activations.

6. Stacking layers  
   • The above block is repeated N times (e.g., 6–96 layers).  
   • Because attention is global each time, deeper layers can refine increasingly abstract relationships.

7. Encoder–decoder structure (for tasks like translation)  
   • Encoder: a stack of attention/FFN blocks reads the source sequence and produces contextual representations.  
   • Decoder: another stack generates the target sequence, with two attention kinds:  
     – Masked self-attention (so it can’t peek at future tokens it hasn’t generated yet).  
     – Cross-attention, which lets each generated token attend to the encoder’s output.

8. Training vs. inference  
   • Training: the model sees full sequences and is optimized (often with cross-entropy loss) to predict the next token.  
   • Inference: it generates tokens one by one, feeding its own outputs back in.

Why it works conceptually  
• Attention removes the bottleneck of sequential processing; dependencies of any length are one step away.  
• Multi-head attention gives multiple “views” of the data simultaneously.  
• Stacking lets the model build hierarchical abstractions, somewhat like layers in a CNN build spatial hierarchies.  
• Residuals and normalization keep deep networks trainable.
